content: Lassa fever is caused by the Lassa virus, which belongs to the Arenaviridae family of zoonotic viruses. This virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus with a bisegmented genome. The natural reservoir of the Lassa virus is the rodent species Mastomys natalensis, commonly referred to as the multimammate rat or mouse. These rodents excrete the virus in their urine and feces, facilitating its transmission. The Lassa virus is classified taxonomically as a single-stranded RNA virus with a negative-sense genome, belonging to the Arenaviridae family and the genus Mammarenavirus. Members of the Arenaviridae family are typically associated with rodent-transmitted diseases in humans, making them zoonotic pathogens. Each virus in this family is generally linked to a specific rodent host species, which serves as its natural reservoir. Structurally, the Lassa virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus with a bisegmented, ambisense genome. Its genome is divided into two RNA segments, each encoding two viral proteins, for a total of four viral proteins. The large segment encodes the RNA polymerase (L protein) and a small zinc-binding protein (Z protein), which regulate transcription and replication. The small segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and the surface glycoprotein precursor (GP). The glycoprotein precursor is cleaved into two envelope glycoproteins, GP1 and GP2, which bind to the alpha-dystroglycan receptor on host cells and mediate viral entry. Genomic studies have identified four distinct lineages of the Lassa virus. Three of these lineages are found in Nigeria, while the fourth is present in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The primary natural reservoir of the Lassa virus is the Mastomys natalensis rodent. This species is notable for its multiple and prominent mammary glands, which give it the name multimammate rat/mouse. These rodents are abundant in the savannas and forests of West, Central, and East Africa. Once infected, Mastomys natalensis can excrete the virus in its urine and feces for extended periods. These rodents breed frequently, produce large litters, and often inhabit human homes, particularly in areas where food is stored. These factors contribute significantly to the efficient transmission of the Lassa virus from infected rodents to humans. Images illustrating key features of the Lassa virus are available from the Public Health Image Library (PHIL) of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
